title: La Junta Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: La Junta wells have a 40-foot median depth, but records range to 798 feet. See yields, costs, permits and risks before buying.
h1: What La Junta Well Records Tell You Before You Buy
intro_html:
La Junta sits on the plains, where nearby well records show a wide spread in drilling conditions. The median reported depth is 40 feet, but the middle half runs from 30 to 462 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 798 feet. That range matters when you compare land prices, request a drilling bid or evaluate an existing home.

This page covers permitted wells within 5 miles of La Junta in Otero County. The records include 924 wells, but only 626 report total depth, 81 report pump yield and 21 report static water level. Treat the statistics as local evidence, not a guarantee for one parcel.

sections.heading: La Junta well depths vary sharply across the plains
sections.html:
Most reported La Junta wells are shallow: 70% are under 100 feet. That pulls the median down to 40 feet. The rest of the records show why a simple average would be misleading: 18% fall between 300 and 600 feet, and 11% exceed 600 feet. Only 1% are in the 100-to-300-foot range.

The local geology is described as alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, with many permits naming an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. A driller should still price the specific lot, not assume the median. For a bid, ask what happens if the hole must go substantially deeper than 40 feet, and confirm which casing and grout work is included.

sections.heading: Reported La Junta yields are generally strong, with limited records
sections.html:
The 81 wells that report pump yield show a median of 18.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 12.0 to 119.0 gallons per minute, a broad spread that reflects different uses and formations. In that reporting group, 68% produce more than 15 gallons per minute, while 31% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, and 1% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. That is encouraging, but it is not a guarantee of household performance because yield reporting is incomplete. Have an existing well tested, and ask a driller about sustained production, storage and recovery rather than relying only on a short pump test.

sections.heading: La Junta water levels look shallow, but the record is too thin for a trend
sections.html:
Only 21 permits report a static water level. Their median depth to water is 15 feet, with the middle half between 4 and 48 feet. Those measurements suggest that water can be relatively shallow in parts of the local area, but they do not establish the water level at a particular property.

The permit counts by decade describe drilling activity, not a water-table trend. Records rise to 204 permits in the 1990s, then show 135 in the 2000s, 39 in the 2010s and 32 in the 2020s. That pattern cannot prove that the water table is dropping or stable. Request current measurements and review nearby wells before closing.

sections.heading: Permit history runs from older irrigation wells to current work
sections.html:
La Junta’s permit record reaches back to the 1950s, when 62 permits were issued. The record shows 64 in the 1960s, 54 in the 1970s, 45 in the 1980s, and the largest decade total, 204, in the 1990s. The newest permit year in the data is 2025.

The most frequently listed drillers are Authorized, shown as 89 wells, Hoffman, Earl, with 75, and Crandall, H A, with 55. These are permit-record names, not endorsements. A new project still requires a Colorado DWR permit review, site-specific access planning and confirmation that the proposed use is allowed. Domestic, stock and irrigation uses appear in the local records, so the permit type deserves close attention.

sections.heading: A La Junta well budget depends more on depth than the median suggests
sections.html:
For alluvium and plains sedimentary rock near La Junta, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 40 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $1,400 to $2,200. That is only the hole, not a functioning water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $7,400 to $14,200 at the median depth. The middle-half depth range of 30 to 462 feet shows why two nearby lots can receive very different bids. Ask for separate line items for drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, power, trenching and testing. Confirm how the contractor handles a dry hole or a hole that must be deepened.

sections.heading: What to check around a La Junta property
sections.html:
Water quantity is only one risk. Within about 10 miles, the mapped records include 18 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 8 historic mine features and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A mapped site does not automatically mean a property’s well is contaminated, but it is a reason to test the water and understand the direction of groundwater movement.

Have a buyer’s water test cover the concerns appropriate to the property and its history. Inspect the wellhead, casing, grout, pressure system and records. Check septic setbacks, available building area, access for a rig and power costs before buying. A shallow water level does not remove the need for proper sanitary protection, and a good yield does not make untreated water safe.

sections.heading: Due diligence for a lot in La Junta, North La Junta or nearby
sections.html:
Start by pulling the DWR permit and construction records for the parcel and neighboring wells. The local area includes La Junta Gardens and North La Junta, both about 2 miles away, Swink at about 5 miles, Cheraw at about 9 miles, Rocky Ford at about 11 miles and Sugar City at about 19 miles. The closest wells usually provide the most useful comparison, especially when their depths, uses and aquifers match the proposed site.

For a home, verify the permit allows the intended household use and ask whether an augmentation plan is needed in an over-appropriated basin. Colorado exempt household-use wells have a 35 gallons-per-minute pumping limit. Before building, obtain a written drilling estimate, confirm septic and driveway layouts, and budget for a range rather than the 40-foot median. For an existing house, make the sale contingent on records, inspection, water testing and a production test.

faq.q: How deep are wells in La Junta?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near La Junta is 40 feet. The middle half runs from 30 to 462 feet. Most, or 70%, are under 100 feet, but 11% exceed 600 feet, with the deepest record at 798 feet. A nearby well record is more useful than the median for pricing one parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in La Junta?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 40-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $1,400 to $2,200. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $7,400 to $14,200. Deeper wells in the local 30-to-462-foot middle-half range can cost substantially more.

faq.q: How much water do La Junta wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 81 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 18.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 12.0 to 119.0 gallons per minute. 68% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Because yield data is limited, a buyer should obtain a production test and review storage and recovery before relying on a well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in La Junta?
faq.a: The well records do not establish drinking-water safety. Within about 10 miles are 18 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 8 historic mine features and 7 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those maps do not prove contamination at a particular well. Test the water, inspect the well construction and review the property’s land-use history before drinking it.

faq.q: Do I need a permit to drill a well near La Junta?
faq.a: Colorado well work is regulated through DWR permits, and the local records include domestic, stock, irrigation and monitoring wells. The correct permit depends on the proposed use, location and water-rights conditions. Exempt household-use wells have a 35-gallons-per-minute pumping limit. Confirm the permit path and any augmentation-plan requirement before buying land or starting construction.
